title: The interval-product spine test for Segal spaces
statement:
Use simplicial spaces, $F(n)$, $cK$, mapping simplicial sets $\operatorname{Map}$ and the Reedy model structure as in [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian]. For $n\geq2$, let $G(n)\subseteq F(n)$ be the union of the images of the $n$ consecutive-edge inclusions $F(1)\to F(n)$, where the $i$th inclusion is induced by $[1]\to[n]$, $0\mapsto i$, $1\mapsto i+1$, for $0\leq i<n$. Let $V$ be a small Reedy fibrant simplicial space whose consecutive-edge comparison $V_m\to V_1\times_{V_0}\cdots\times_{V_0}V_1$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every $m\geq2$. Then, for every $n\geq2$, restriction along $F(1)\times G(n)\hookrightarrow F(1)\times F(n)$ induces a weak homotopy equivalence
$$\operatorname{Map}(F(1)\times F(n),V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(F(1)\times G(n),V).$$

source.place: Rezk, A model for the homotopy theory of homotopy theory, Lemma 10.3 and its proof via Lemma 10.1 and diagram (10.4), printed pp. 23-24; local equivalence is interpreted by Theorem 7.1(3), constructed before proving cartesian compatibility. Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this simplicial-space result.

proof.text: Fix $n\geq2$ and put $P=F(1)\times F(n)$ and $A=F(1)\times G(n)$. For $0\leq i\leq n$, define the injective monotone map $\gamma_i:[n+1]\to[1]\times[n]$ by $\gamma_i(j)=(0,j)$ for $j\leq i$ and $\gamma_i(j)=(1,j-1)$ for $j>i$. Write $C_i$ for its simplex image and $U_i=\bigcup_{j=0}^iC_j$. For $0\leq i<n$, define $\delta_i:[n]\to[1]\times[n]$ by $\delta_i(j)=(0,j)$ for $j\leq i$ and $(1,j)$ for $j>i$, and write $D_i$ for its image. Any simplex of $P$ is a weakly increasing chain of pairs. If the chain has a one-row vertex, choose $i$ to be the least second coordinate of its one-row vertices; otherwise choose $i=n$. Monotonicity makes every zero-row second coordinate at most $i$, and every one-row second coordinate at least $i$. These are precisely the vertex bounds for $C_i$, so the chain belongs to $C_i$. Thus $U_n=P$. For $i>0$, $C_i\cap U_{i-1}=D_{i-1}$: a chain common to $C_i$ and an earlier $C_j$ has zero-row second coordinates at most $i-1$ and one-row second coordinates at least $i$, so lies in $D_{i-1}$; conversely $D_{i-1}\subseteq C_{i-1}\cap C_i$. Therefore $U_i=U_{i-1}\amalg_{D_{i-1}}C_i$, and intersection with $A$ gives the corresponding pushout of subobjects.

source.place: Lemma 10.3, prism chains and diagram (10.4); degreewise verification

proof.text: Pull $A\cap C_i$ back along $\gamma_i$. Let $p_i:[n+1]\to[n]$ be its second coordinate: $p_i(j)=j$ for $j\leq i$ and $j-1$ for $j>i$. The pullback is exactly the union of interval faces on the consecutive vertex sets $p_i^{-1}(\{r,r+1\})$, $0\leq r<n$. Indeed a chain is in $G(n)$ precisely when its second-coordinate values lie in a single consecutive edge. Each preimage is a consecutive interval with at least two vertices. Every consecutive pair $j,j+1$ is in one such interval, since $p_i(j+1)-p_i(j)$ is either zero or one; in the zero case its common value belongs to at least one edge of $[n]$, including at the endpoints. Thus this union contains $G(n+1)$. The second coordinate of $\delta_i$ is the identity, so $A\cap D_i$ pulls back to $G(n)$. Apply [lem-coef-segal-interval-cover] with $m=n+1$ to each $C_i$, and with $m=n$, $H=G(n)$ to each $D_i$. Its hypotheses hold for the given $V$. We obtain weak homotopy equivalences $\operatorname{Map}(C_i,V)\to\operatorname{Map}(A\cap C_i,V)$ and $\operatorname{Map}(D_i,V)\to\operatorname{Map}(A\cap D_i,V)$ for all their indicated indices.

source.place: Lemma 10.3, interval-face calculation; Lemma 10.1 with explicit spine hypothesis

proof.text:
For $i>0$, applying $\operatorname{Map}(-,V)$ to the two pushouts of step 1 identifies their mapping simplicial sets with strict pullbacks:
$$\operatorname{Map}(U_i,V)=\operatorname{Map}(C_i,V)\times_{\operatorname{Map}(D_{i-1},V)}\operatorname{Map}(U_{i-1},V),$$
$$\operatorname{Map}(A\cap U_i,V)=\operatorname{Map}(A\cap C_i,V)\times_{\operatorname{Map}(A\cap D_{i-1},V)}\operatorname{Map}(A\cap U_{i-1},V).$$
These identifications hold in every simplicial degree: a map out of a union is exactly a pair of maps agreeing on its intersection, also after product with $c\Delta^q$. The first legs of both cospans, restrictions from $C_i$ and $A\cap C_i$ to the respective overlaps, are Kan fibrations by [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian], applied to those monomorphisms and the Reedy fibration $V\to *$. The mapping space into $*$ is terminal, so its displayed relative mapping-fibration assertion has exactly these absolute restrictions as its instances.

source.place: Sections 2.3-2.5, mapping enrichment and restriction fibrations; Lemma 10.3 gluing

proof.text: Induct on $i$ to prove that restriction $\operatorname{Map}(U_i,V)\to\operatorname{Map}(A\cap U_i,V)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. At $i=0$ this is the $C_0$ assertion of step 2. For $i>0$, compare the cospans in step 3. The maps on the first objects and on their bases are weak equivalences by step 2, and the maps on the last objects are weak equivalences by the induction hypothesis. The restriction maps form a commuting map of cospans by precomposition, and their first legs are both Kan fibrations by step 3. The strict-pullback assertion of [lem-coef-kan-pullback-fibration-invariance] therefore gives the induction step. At $i=n$, $U_n=P$ and $A\cap U_n=A$, so this is precisely the restriction map in the statement. No cartesian compatibility of the Segal-local model structure or assertion about $V^{F(1)}$ has been used.

source.place: Lemma 10.3, comparison of diagram (10.4), with the finite gluing induction supplied
